response.passage: In India, every citizen who is 18 years of age or older has the right to vote, regardless of their level of education or the property they own. To ensure that the process remains private, the voting system is designed as a secret ballot. When you go to a polling station, you cast your vote on an Electronic Voting Machine (EVM). These machines are standalone devices and are not connected to the internet or any external network, which keeps them secure from remote hacking. After you press the button for your chosen candidate, a Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail (VVPAT) machine prints a slip showing your choice for a few seconds behind a glass window, which then drops into a sealed box inside the machine. You do not take this slip home; it stays with the election officials for verification. Furthermore, the Election Commission is an independent body that functions separately from the ruling government to ensure fair elections. While voting is a vital duty for every citizen to strengthen democracy, it is not legally compulsory, and no one is fined or punished for not casting their vote. Finally, the NOTA option allows voters to express that they do not wish to support any candidate, but it does not trigger a re-election if it receives the most votes.
response.summary: India's democratic process relies on independent oversight and secure, private voting methods. Every adult citizen has the right to vote, though it remains a voluntary civic duty rather than a legal requirement.
